s1.title: The higher timeframe decides first
s1.takeaway: No trade without looking up: read the higher timeframe first, then trade the lower one.
s1.body: Before you read a pattern or a signal on your trading timeframe, read the one above it: in Elder's triple-screen sense you never trade against the higher timeframe — you trade with it or not at all. “4h bearish” commits you: shorts are the plan, longs need above-average evidence and tighter targets, and invalidation sits at the 4h structure, not on your 5m candle.
s1.chartHint: The chart below follows the same logic as the indicator lessons, timeframe switch included: flip from 4h to 5m and watch the same reading change its story — the lower timeframe chops where the higher one still has direction.

s2.title: Structure: reading breaks, not guessing
s2.takeaway: Name the break: BOS means continuation, CHOCH means caution — always relative to your swings.
s2.body: An uptrend is a sequence of rising highs and lows; when price breaks the last low, that is a break of structure (BOS) — the trend continues downward. When it then breaks against the new direction, that is a change of character (CHOCH): not a signal, but the first warning that the other side is back in the game. Swing highs and lows are not measurements: every trader draws them differently, and whoever sees different swings sees different breaks — a BOS only ever holds relative to the swings you chose. The sketch shows the pattern drawn cleanly once, including the zone that changes sides after the break. Whether the break holds is decided by the retest — no indicator takes that from you.

s3.title: Levels that persist
s3.takeaway: Only trade zones from the higher timeframe; the rest is noise.
s3.body: Support and resistance are not lines on the chart but zones where a lot traded earlier: old swing zones, flip zones after a BOS — and the higher the timeframe, the more they carry. When resistance breaks it becomes support: not out of geometry, but because the sellers of that time sit in loss there and want out on the retest. That is why levels outlive their candles: what was a level on 4h still is one when the 5m candles have long fallen off the window. Trade levels from the higher timeframe and manage the entry on the lower — the same division of labor as with bias.

s4a.title: Trend or range
s4a.takeaway: When ADX rises, follow the trend; when it stays flat or Choppiness runs high, trade the range — or stand aside.
s4a.body: Trend or range decides which tools are readable at all: when ADX rises above roughly 25, trend-following toward the top DI line pays; when it falls, or Choppiness sits above 61.8, breakouts fail and oscillator extremes gain meaning. None of this classifies the market for you: these are readings, each with a flip side — strong in trend, blind in range, and vice versa.

s4b.title: Expansion
s4b.takeaway: Compression means movement without direction, expansion means wider stops — adjust your size, not your view.
s4b.body: Bandwidth at its lowest announces movement, not direction — a setup without a side is half a setup. ATR says how large the normal move currently is: as it expands, stops and targets must grow with it, or ordinary noise eats the trade. The buttons below open the lessons that teach each reading in detail.

adx.whatItMeasures: Trend strength in three parts. +DI and −DI say which side is dominant; ADX says how strong that dominance is — it is itself the smoothed difference between the two. One period governs both the directional smoothing and ADX's own window. ADX carries no direction of its own.
adx.howToRead: ADX above roughly 25 is conventionally read as trending, below 20 as not. Direction matters more than level: a rising ADX rewards trend-following toward the top DI line — the DI cross is the timing, the ADX decides whether it counts. A falling ADX means the trend is weakening, even while the reading is still high. Read it as a filter on the other two: +DI above −DI with ADX high is a directional read worth acting on; +DI above −DI with ADX low is not. A rising ADX says movement is intensifying — never that it is upward. The separation of strength from direction is the whole design of this indicator.
adx.failureModes: It is not directional, and reading it that way is the main error — the number answers how strongly one side is winning, never which side. It is lagged by construction, an average of an average, so by the time it reads high the move has been running for a while. It can read high inside a range, because a violent two-way market produces directional movement on both sides and the absolute movement ADX measures does not tell those apart. The 20 and 25 thresholds are conventions rather than properties: they come from experience with particular instruments and periods, and nothing breaks when price disagrees with them.
adx.confirmation: Nothing confirms it on its own. Used alone it is close to useless — it is the filter that decides whether the trend indicators are worth reading at all.

bollinger.whatItMeasures: An SMA(20) of closing prices with two bands two standard deviations above and below it. Five outputs: upper, middle and lower, %B (where price sits within the band span, 0 at the lower band and 1 at the upper — allowed to run beyond), and bandwidth (the span as a percentage of the middle band).
bollinger.howToRead: Price riding the upper band in a trend is continuation, not exhaustion — the single most consequential reading in this family and the one most often taught backwards. A close beyond the band with the trend flattening is a genuine warning instead — same place, different trend state. Bandwidth at its lowest is a compression: it marks that a move is coming, not which way. %B answers where price sits inside the envelope, which is what separates a close below 0 under a rising lower band from one in a falling market.
bollinger.failureModes: bandwidth is scaled by 100 and printed as a percentage, and this is the one that causes real losses. A reading of 2.41 means 2.41 percent, not the bare ratio 0.0241 that is the common convention elsewhere — a condition written as bandwidth < 2.41 on that convention is true on nearly every candle and fires constantly. Touching a band is not a signal: in a trend price touches the bands continuously and stays there, so bands describe the envelope of recent variation rather than a boundary. Two standard deviations is a parameter, not a law, and a wider setting widens the envelope without making it more correct. %B is undefined when the band width is zero, which is a real condition on a completely flat stretch. Compression resolves in a direction this indicator cannot tell you, so presenting bandwidth as a setup is presenting half of one.
bollinger.confirmation: A range to trade, or expansion being read. As a regime filter for the trend family: a squeeze says trend-following signals are not yet worth acting on.

ema.whatItMeasures: The exponentially weighted average of closing prices over the last N periods: recent prices count most, older ones fade out instead of dropping out of the window at once. Drawn as a line over the price.
ema.howToRead: Price above a rising average means buyers have been paying up recently; below a falling one means the opposite. Slope matters more than level — a flat average is not a trend statement in either direction. Distance from the average measures how extended price is, not how likely it is to return.
ema.failureModes: Faster is not more informative. A short-period EMA produces more signals than a long one — and in a range that is strictly worse: more chances to be wrong, none of them more correct. Because the average is built from past prices, a cross always arrives after the move it confirms. The faster the average, the higher the false-cross rate: the earlier signal is bought with reliability, not given away. In a range it is a trend line drawn through noise — crosses fire repeatedly and each one says nothing. On a short history a long-period EMA exists and draws, but describes almost nothing about the regime.
ema.confirmation: Trend definition and dynamic support: a rising average supports, a falling one caps. Settle the regime question before every cross — adx and choppiness decide whether an average's crosses should be believed at all.

sma.whatItMeasures: The average of closing prices over the last N periods, every period weighted the same — the oldest point drops out completely with each new one. Drawn as a line over the price.
sma.howToRead: Price above a rising average means buyers have been paying up recently; below a falling one means the opposite. Slope matters more than level — a flat average is not a trend statement in either direction. Distance from the average measures how extended price is, not how likely it is to return.
sma.failureModes: The lag is the highest of the four averages and it does not shrink with tuning: doubling the period doubles how far behind the move the line sits. And it barks twice: once when a new price comes in — as it should — and once when an old one drops out. When an old extreme leaves the window, the line buckles as if in a downtrend, though the market has not moved. At N=10 every day weighs 10%, at N=200 only 0.5%. Because the average is built from past prices, a cross always arrives after the move it confirms, so the entry arrives late by construction. In a range it is a trend line drawn through noise — crosses fire repeatedly and each one says nothing. On a short history a long-period SMA exists and draws, but describes almost nothing about the regime.
sma.confirmation: Trend definition and dynamic support: a rising average supports, a falling one caps. Settle the regime question before every cross — adx and choppiness decide whether an average's crosses should be believed at all.

wma.whatItMeasures: The average of closing prices over the last N periods, weighted linearly towards the newest period: the newest day counts N times, then N-1 and so on, divided by their sum — 55 at N=10. A compromise between the equal weighting of the SMA and the heavy recent weighting of the EMA.
wma.howToRead: Price above a rising average means buyers have been paying up recently; below a falling one means the opposite. Slope matters more than level — a flat average is not a trend statement in either direction. Distance from the average measures how extended price is, not how likely it is to return.
wma.failureModes: It has no failure mode of its own, which is worth saying plainly: between the SMA and the EMA it inherits both — the lag of the former, the noise sensitivity of the latter. Choosing it is a bet on noise tolerance, not a choice of accuracy, and nothing distinguishes it in reliability from an EMA of comparable period. Linear weighting solves only the weighting problem, not the window problem: when an old value drops out, the WMA jumps too — smaller than the SMA, since the oldest point carries weight 1 only, but for the same reason. In a range it is a trend line drawn through noise — crosses fire repeatedly and each one says nothing. On a short history a long-period WMA exists and draws, but describes almost nothing about the regime.
wma.confirmation: Trend definition and dynamic support: a rising average supports, a falling one caps. Settle the regime question before every cross — adx and choppiness decide whether an average's crosses should be believed at all.

hma.whatItMeasures: An average of closing prices built from two linearly weighted averages: double the half-period WMA, subtract the full-period one, and smooth the result over the square root of the period. That removes nearly all lag. The fastest and the noisiest of the four moving averages.
hma.howToRead: Price above a rising average means buyers have been paying up recently; below a falling one means the opposite. Slope matters more than level — a flat average is not a trend statement in either direction. Distance from the average measures how extended price is, not how likely it is to return.
hma.failureModes: The lag reduction is paid for in noise. HMA turns sooner and therefore says more, and in a range saying more is strictly worse — more chances to be wrong, none of them more correct. Its closeness to price is the strength in a clean trend and the weakness in a range: it turns on every twitch — many small false turns instead of few large ones. In a range it is a trend line drawn through noise — crosses fire repeatedly and each one says nothing. On a short history a long-period HMA exists and draws, but describes almost nothing about the regime.
hma.confirmation: Trend definition and dynamic support: a rising average supports, a falling one caps. Settle the regime question before every cross — adx and choppiness decide whether an average's crosses should be believed at all.

vwma.whatItMeasures: The average of closing prices over N periods, weighted by traded volume rather than by recency: the heaviest-traded periods count most.
vwma.howToRead: Where the average sits against price is read as with any other average — but it now reflects where trading actually happened rather than only where price went. While price holds above a rising VWMA, most volume transacted lower: the buying majority sits in profit. Breaks below it, and the accumulated volume flips to the losing side.
vwma.failureModes: A single block — one print, one participant — moves the line more than a week of price. That is intended and also the failure: the average follows it, though no broad consensus needs to stand behind it. It inherits every moving-average failure and adds sensitivity to volume data quality on top, which a plain average does not have. And it is not the session VWAP: this average rolls over N periods, is anchored nowhere, and is no benchmark. It is not a volume indicator and confirms nothing by itself — it is a price average with a different weighting, and reading it as volume participation is reading the wrong thing.
vwma.confirmation: Levels where volume concentration matters. Compare it against an unweighted average rather than using it instead of one.

macd.whatItMeasures: The difference between a fast (12) and a slow (26) EMA on closing prices, plus a signal line (a 9-period EMA of that difference) and the histogram (the gap between the two). Two lines plus bars on a separate axis below the price, with the zero line emphasised.
macd.howToRead: The sign of the MACD line says which side's average is higher — direction. The MACD/signal cross is the event most systems use. The histogram says how fast that gap is opening or closing, which is a statement about the current move rather than about direction. A histogram turning ahead of the cross is early warning, not a signal. Divergence — price with a new high or low, MACD and histogram without — is the strongest warning. The best crosses: buys below zero, sells above zero.
macd.failureModes: A shrinking histogram is not a reversal. It means the two averages are converging, which happens in every trend when it pauses, and it says nothing about which way it resolves. The histogram is derived — the difference of the other two by definition — so reading all three as three signals counts one number twice. It lags more than the price does, being built from two averages and therefore later than either. In a range the MACD line spends most of its time near zero, where its sign is noise, and a cross there is the crossing of two lines that are both flat.
macd.confirmation: Direction and momentum shifts on a higher timeframe than the entry.

super_trend.whatItMeasures: A trailing band from period midpoint ± factor·ATR (defaults 10 and 3). Price standing above the band is the trend read as up; the active band flips to the other side when price crosses it. Three outputs: value (the active band), upper and lower (the two candidate bands).
super_trend.howToRead: The flip is the event. The value line is the band the trend currently stands on, not a price level in itself — while the trend holds, it moves only in trend direction or sideways, never back. Direction from the higher timeframe, exit on the lower: on a counter-flip, close, don't reverse.
super_trend.failureModes: The bands are not support. They trail, so they move away from old price, and reading the band as a level price should hold is a category error. It whipsaws in a range, where each flip is a real signal that is wrong; the factor setting controls how much volatility is required to flip, which is a direct dial on how many false flips a range produces. As stop-and-reverse it is not profitable: whether trend or sawtooth follows is known only afterwards. Being volatility-derived, it inherits that too: a volatility spike produces a wide band, and price can stay on the trend side of it through a violent drop whenever the volatility justifies it — the reading can be "still uptrend" mid-crash.
super_trend.confirmation: Trailing trend exits and mechanical trend membership, on a timeframe where the whipsaw rate is acceptable.

parabolic_sar.whatItMeasures: Wilder's point trailing price on the side of the trend: each new extreme grows the acceleration factor (start 0.02, increment 0.02, maximum 0.2), and the point catches up to price. On a cross it switches sides — doubling as the stop-and-reverse point.
parabolic_sar.howToRead: The value line is the SAR point. The direction line is not a price — it is the side the SAR stands on, +1 while it trails below price and −1 while it stands above, so "the SAR flips" is the direction crossing zero. That is exactly where it is useful: the flip is the signal, and a close crossing the SAR itself can miss a reversal on a candle that closes back across.
parabolic_sar.failureModes: Acceleration is the trap. The SAR closes in on price the longer the trend runs — and plants the new SAR at the old extreme after the flip: the further the trend ran, the longer the way back on a false signal. It whipsaws in a range harder than a volatility-filtered trailing band, because there is no volatility filter in its design — only the accelerating step. The direction line is the signal and reading it as a magnitude is meaningless: it has two states. The first point is a seed rather than a reading, appearing only once a second candle exists.
parabolic_sar.confirmation: Mechanical trailing stops in a trend, where accepting the whipsaw is the accepted cost. Trust it only with a regime filter (adx) — trends cover only a fraction of the time.

ichimoku.whatItMeasures: Four lines in alerts (no Chikou among them — the chart additionally draws the lagging span). The cloud is drawn from two spans and projected forward by 26 periods; tenkan (9, conversion) and kijun (26, base) are not averages but midpoints of their period's high and low. Price relative to the cloud is the trend statement; tenkan relative to kijun is a shorter-term statement within it.
ichimoku.howToRead: Above the cloud — hence above both spans — is an uptrend with support defined by the cloud's lower edge; below it is the mirror image. Tenkan crossing kijun is the timing signal inside the direction.
ichimoku.failureModes: Displacement is fixed, not a setting: the spans are projected forward by a constant and the core computes it that way, so a lesson or an alert presenting it as tunable is describing something that does not exist here. The cloud is a lagging construction, and visibly so: built from midpoints and projected — it is a statement about where price was and how it would have behaved had the trend continued. It needs far more history than the other trend indicators, the longest span runs 52 periods plus 26 displacement, and on a short history the cloud has no established shape — the reading is not interpretable. Four alert lines are a lot to read at once, and the reading most people take — above or below — uses one of them; the rest are refinement. The classic system's fifth line (Chikou) is not available in alerts — only the chart draws the lagging span.
ichimoku.confirmation: Multi-timeframe analysis where the higher timeframe is the reference and the lower one is the entry, on instruments with enough history.

atr.whatItMeasures: Wilder's average true range (default 14): the average of the true range — each period the maximum of the day's span, the high against the prior close and the low against the prior close, smoothed Wilder's way. It measures the magnitude of movement, not direction, and carries no sign.
atr.howToRead: Read against price it says how far the instrument normally travels in a period, and that number is a distance budget: a stop narrower than it is likely to be hit by ordinary movement, a target that is a large multiple of it is ambitious. Read as a percentage of price it compares instruments that trade at different scales.
atr.failureModes: It is not directional and cannot forecast. A high ATR is not "the market will fall" — it is not even a claim about the market, only about its movement. It is absolute rather than relative: a raw reading of 500 is unremarkable on one instrument and enormous on another, and it grows with the price level over months, so comparing the raw reading across instruments or across time compares nothing. It rises after the move — by the time volatility is high it is high because something happened, and used as a prediction it is a lagging statement. It spikes on gaps and shocks and stays elevated after the shock is over, temporarily overstating the normal range.
atr.confirmation: Stop placement and position sizing: think in ATR multiples instead of points. Also the volatility input that makes the SuperTrend band adaptive.

choppiness.whatItMeasures: A single number between 0 and 100 (default 14) summarising how directional the movement is. Near 100 the market has been moving within a narrow, directionless band; near 0 it has been moving decisively in one direction.
choppiness.howToRead: As a regime filter and nothing else. Above the usual thresholds (Dreiss: 61.8): range behaviour, where breakouts fail and oscillator extremes mean something. Below them (38.2): trending, where the oscillators are unreliable and the overlays are the ones worth reading.
choppiness.failureModes: It is not directional. A reading at 90 says the market is not trending, not that it will go down — the same foundational trap as ATR. Around the middle it is noise: the useful information is at the extremes, and a rule that fires on a mid-range reading is acting on the part of the scale that carries nothing. It is calculated over a window and lags, so the regime it describes has often already been left behind by the time it confirms. It classifies movement, not the trader's opportunity — a high reading means trend-following is not indicated, not that range-trading is.
choppiness.confirmation: Gating the other lessons. Used as a precondition on a signal rather than as a signal itself.

rsi.whatItMeasures: Relative strength of gains versus losses, as a value between 0 and 100. 50 marks the balance between buyers and sellers. It uses Wilder smoothing over the configured period — 14 by default. Shorter periods react faster and choppier, longer ones slower and calmer. Computed from closing prices by default, from another price source where that is meaningful.
rsi.howToRead: Readings above 50 lean toward buyers, readings below 50 toward sellers. That is a tendency, not a signal. The outer marks at 70 and 30 flag a move stretched against its own recent history — convention, not buy or sell signals. The most reliable reading is usually the shape, not the level. Regular divergence — price makes a higher high while RSI makes a lower high, or price a lower low while RSI a higher low — points to a possible reversal. Hidden divergence — price makes a higher low while RSI makes a lower low in an uptrend, or a lower high while RSI makes a higher high in a downtrend — points to continuation. Either counts only where the chart already gives the move a reason: at a boundary, after a break, at a level that already matters.
rsi.failureModes: In a trending market it stays above 70 or below 30 for as long as the trend lasts. In a strong uptrend it reads overbought on almost every candle. Trading that as a sell signal collects small losses against one large move. Inside a range, divergence appears all the time. Two highs between the same levels still produce a divergence. Divergence claims momentum is failing — in a range there is no momentum to fail. Overbought means stretched against recent history, not expensive in absolute terms. A new high can be healthy; the reading only says the climb was fast. Shorter periods reach the outer marks sooner and fail sooner in trends. When the price did not move at all inside the window, there is no RSI value. The lesson shows indeterminate instead of a number.
rsi.confirmation: Reversal setups at range boundaries, with a defined stop beyond the level. Let the boundary confirm: a level that holds, a candle that rejects, room before the next barrier. Trend continuation is not its job — an overlay drawn on the price itself carries that signal.

stoch_rsi.whatItMeasures: The stochastic of the RSI: the stochastic's position-within-range logic applied to RSI values rather than to price. %K and %D, both between 0 and 100, say where RSI currently sits within its own configured range. Computed over the configured periods — 14 for the RSI and the range and 3 for each smoothing by default. Shorter ranges react faster and choppier, longer ones slower and calmer.
stoch_rsi.howToRead: Crosses of %K over %D are the usual event. 80 and 20 are the customary outer marks — convention, not buy or sell signals. The middle line at 50 splits the range in two halves: above it, the RSI stands in its upper half. A cross above it confirms the direction of the RSI push. That is no buy or sell signal either. Read it as a statement about where the RSI is inside its own range, not as a statement about price.
stoch_rsi.failureModes: Double smoothing reaches its extremes more often than the underlying RSI does. Readings that would be rare on the RSI are routine here. The transform that makes it responsive is what makes it noisy. In a trend it sticks to the extremes instead of warning of the turn: at 100 in an uptrend, at 0 in a downtrend, for as long as the trend lasts. It inherits every RSI failure and adds one: the extra step removes the absolute level information that would have told you which regime you are in. Its range is RSI-relative, not price-relative. At the top of its range refers to where RSI is, not to where price is. A strongly rising price can sit at a low stochastic when the RSI has been rising faster still. Shorter ranges reach the outer marks sooner and fail sooner in trends. When the RSI did not move at all inside the range, there is no value. The lesson shows indeterminate instead of a number.
stoch_rsi.confirmation: Very short mean-reversion entries in genuinely quiet conditions. A precision tool for a narrow case, not a general-purpose oscillator.

stochastic.whatItMeasures: Where the close sits within the highest high and lowest low of the configured window. %K is that position smoothed, %D is a moving average of %K. Both run between 0 and 100. Computed from high, low and close over the configured periods — 14 for the window and 3 for each smoothing by default. With smoothing it shows the slow variant in the default setting, the calmer one with the more reliable signals. Shorter windows react faster and choppier, longer ones slower and calmer.
stochastic.howToRead: A %K above 80 means the close sits near the top of the configured window's range. Below 20 it sits near the bottom. Those are positions, not signals. 80 and 20 are the customary marks — convention, not buy or sell signals. The event most systems are built on is %K crossing %D. The strongest reading is divergence as with the RSI, read on the %D line in the extreme zone: when %D forms falling peaks while price keeps rising, or rising troughs while price keeps falling, that warns of the turn. Reading that as the market being nearly finished rising or falling confuses the window with the market: the statement covers the configured window, not the future.
stochastic.failureModes: In a trend it fails permanently — that is the defining failure. In a sustained uptrend the close keeps sitting near the window high, and %K stays above 80 for the length of the trend. Selling every overbought print in a trend is systematically short the only move that matters. Mirrored, the same holds in a downtrend: the close sits near the window low, %K stays below 20, and buying every oversold reading is systematically long against the only move that matters. The window is the claim: at the top means the top of the configured candles, and a different setting produces a different reading of the same chart. No setting is more correct than another. %D trails %K by construction. A cross can be well underway before it prints. Shorter windows reach the outer marks sooner and fail sooner in trends. When the price did not move at all inside the window, there is no value. The lesson shows indeterminate instead of a number.
stochastic.confirmation: Range trading at established boundaries, with a market-structure read that establishes the boundary first. Without one, it is guessing where the range ends.

williams_r.whatItMeasures: The close's position within the configured range, scaled to −100…0 rather than 0…100. The same calculation as the stochastic, only shifted and inverted. Computed from high, low and close over the configured period — 14 by default. Shorter windows react faster and choppier, longer ones slower and calmer.
williams_r.howToRead: 0 is the top of the window's range, −100 the bottom. −20 and −80 are the customary outer marks — convention, not buy or sell signals. Divergence reads as with the stochastic, at the outer marks, not in the middle. Every stochastic caveat applies unchanged — read it as a member of that family, not as a separate idea.
williams_r.failureModes: Everything the stochastic does, for the same reasons. Plus one failure specific to how it is usually used: it is not a second, independent opinion. It is the same calculation on a different scale. Treating two correlated readings as two confirmations overstates the evidence. That is how a position ends up sized as though it had two reasons and has one. When the price did not move at all inside the window, there is no value. The lesson shows indeterminate instead of a number.
williams_r.confirmation: Wherever the stochastic fits. Choosing one over the other is a display preference, not an analytical one.

cci.whatItMeasures: How far the typical price sits from its own moving average, expressed in statistical units. The 0.015 divisor is calibrated so that roughly 70 to 80 percent of all readings land between −100 and +100. The typical price is the average of high, low and close. Computed over the configured period — 20 by default — from the typical price by default, from another price source where that is meaningful. Shorter periods react faster and choppier, longer ones slower and calmer.
cci.howToRead: ±100 is the statistically ordinary excursion. Beyond roughly ±200 the move is unusual relative to its own recent behaviour. Those are conventions, not buy or sell signals. The sign tells you which side is active. Divergence reads as with the RSI, at the ±200 zones, not in the middle. The lines at ±100 and ±200 belong on the chart, because they make the scale's assumption visible instead of leaving it implied.
cci.failureModes: The ±100 band assumes a stable distribution. CCI assumes its own recent behaviour is representative. In a trending market the price spends most of its time outside ±100. Not because the move is unusual, but because recent behaviour no longer describes the market. It is unbounded, unlike the family it usually stands beside. A reading outside ±200 is not a reversal signal and not an exhaustion signal. It means the scale's assumption is violated. Typical price averages away the wick, so on a candle where the rejection was entirely in the high or the low, CCI can read mild. When the price did not move at all inside the window, there is no value. The lesson shows indeterminate instead of a number.
cci.confirmation: Momentum entries after a genuine directional break, where the question is how strong this is rather than how far it has already gone.

mfi.whatItMeasures: The relative-strength calculation applied to the typical price using volume as the weighting. An RSI on volume-weighted price rather than on price alone. Computed over the configured period — 14 by default. Shorter periods react faster and choppier, longer ones slower and calmer.
mfi.howToRead: Same shape as the RSI. Readings above 50 lean toward buyers. That is a tendency, not a signal. 80 and 20 are the customary outer marks — convention, not buy or sell signals. The addition over the RSI: the same price move on heavy volume produces a more extreme reading than on thin volume. That is the intended signal. The MFI-native signal is the failure swing: when it rises above 80, pulls back, fails to reach the old peak on the second attempt and then breaks the intervening trough, that warns of the turn. Mirrored, the same holds at the bottom.
mfi.failureModes: It is not a volume indicator. It does not measure participation. It measures price change weighted by volume. A single enormous volume spike on a flat candle moves it with no price change at all. It inherits every RSI failure, trend case included, in full. Volume is the input most likely to be wrong or absent. On a thin or fragmented symbol the weighting is unreliable in ways the reading does not reveal. That matters more here than for any price-only indicator. When no money flowed either way inside the window — no movement or no volume — there is no value. The lesson shows indeterminate instead of a number.
mfi.confirmation: Divergence and failure-swing work where volume confirmation is specifically wanted.

ao.whatItMeasures: The difference between a fast and a slow simple average of the median price. The median price is the bar's midpoint of high and low. Rises when short-term movement exceeds long-term, falls when it does not. Computed over the configured periods — 5 and 34 by default.
ao.howToRead: The zero line is the whole signal. Above it, short-term movement dominates. There are no useful fixed thresholds. Unlike the RSI, no 70 means anything: the scale runs in price units and moves with the instrument. Compare slope and duration above or below the line instead. The classic signals: a cross of the zero line. Saucer: the bars turn from down to up above the line. Twin peaks: two troughs below the line, the second shallower, confirmed by the next rising bar. Mirrored, everything holds below.
ao.failureModes: It carries no scale. A reading of +40 on one symbol and +4,000 on another mean the same thing proportionally and different things absolutely. Any threshold quoted without naming the instrument is meaningless. That is the most common failure with this indicator: adopting a fixed threshold sight unseen. It is structurally lagged. Both inputs are smoothed. Turns in the underlying movement appear in the reading after they happened. The median price is the bar's midpoint, not its close: a rejection in the wick moves the high or the low and hence the reading, even when the close barely moves. Before a full window of the slower period there is no value. The lesson shows indeterminate instead of a number.
ao.confirmation: Confirming direction and relative strength on a higher timeframe than the entry, where the question is which side is in control.

momentum.whatItMeasures: The closing price against the closing price a configured period back, as a difference. No averaging is involved at any stage. Computed over the configured period — 10 by default — from closing prices by default, from another price source where that is meaningful. Shorter periods react faster and choppier, longer ones slower and calmer.
momentum.howToRead: Sign is direction, magnitude is the gain or loss relative to the base. Because nothing is smoothed, the reading is as fast as the market. The most important reading is the slope, not the level: when the line flattens while price still rises, acceleration is fading. When it falls toward the zero line, the intact trend is losing steepness. A cross of the zero line only counts with the trend: upward only in an uptrend, downward only in a downtrend.
momentum.failureModes: It compares two prices a full period apart, and its scale drifts with price. A reading of +500 means something different on every instrument and changes meaning over months on the same one. Quoting a level without context is therefore meaningless here — in a way it is not for a bounded oscillator. For the same reason it is not comparable across instruments. That is precisely what makes the bounded oscillators convenient for alert conditions. Without smoothing the comparison is extremely noisy: the reading reflects one candle's move against another a period apart, which is often noise rather than information. There is also the drop-off effect: when an old extreme falls out of the window — say the spike ten candles back — the line jumps with no movement in the current price.
momentum.confirmation: Fast directional reads where smoothing would be too slow, usually on a higher timeframe than the one being traded.

obv.whatItMeasures: Granville's running total (1963): it adds the volume of every candle closing above the prior close and subtracts the volume of every candle closing below it (an unchanged close counts zero). The line's slope is the reading; the line's level is not.
obv.howToRead: Whether the total is rising or falling while price moves, or fails to. Rising OBV with rising price means the advance is being paid for; rising OBV with falling price means selling is being absorbed. Divergence between price and OBV is the usual event.
obv.failureModes: The level is meaningless, and this is the defining constraint rather than a caveat. OBV is a cumulative total, so its value depends on how much history has been loaded — the same market through a different rolling window produces a different OBV level. Only the slope carries information; comparing the absolute number against a threshold is wrong at the foundation. It is a sign convention rather than a magnitude: a huge down-candle on tiny volume barely moves it while a quiet candle on large volume moves it a lot, so the total reflects volume and candle direction equally, which is not the same as money flow. It cannot be compared against a price — different units, no shared scale, only the direction of change is comparable. It inherits the volume-quality problem: a fragmented or thin volume feed makes it unreliable in ways the number does not reveal.
obv.confirmation: Volume confirmation of a price claim, and divergence work. Read the slope, never the level.

volume_ma.whatItMeasures: The SMA(20) of volume — the moving-average family applied to volume instead of price.
volume_ma.howToRead: How far the current bar's volume sits from what has been normal recently. A breakout on clearly above-normal volume means something different from one on unusually thin volume, and this is what makes that comparison concrete.
volume_ma.failureModes: It has no direction. Volume is unsigned, so it cannot say whether buyers or sellers were active — and "high volume is high volume", not "who was doing it": accumulation and distribution are indistinguishable in this number. "High volume" is relative to itself, so a normal reading during a quiet period is not comparable to a normal reading during an active one, and absolute volume levels are not portable across instruments. It describes the past N periods rather than the current bar, so a spike on the last candle has barely entered the average and comparing the bar against an average that already includes it understates the spike.
volume_ma.confirmation: Sizing the conviction behind a price move, and filtering breakouts whose volume does not support them.

refusal.executableTextRejected: A strategy is checkable data, not executable text. Free-text expressions are refused.
refusal.unsupportedSchemaVersion: This rule uses a schema version this build of the app cannot read.
refusal.migrationNotPossible: The rule cannot be carried to the current schema version with its meaning intact, so it is refused rather than reinterpreted.
refusal.emptyConditionTree: A group with no conditions has no truth value.
refusal.conditionTreeTooDeep: The conditions are nested too deeply.
refusal.duplicateConditionId: The same condition identifier is used twice.
refusal.invalidLookback: A percentage move needs an earlier candle to measure from. A lookback of 0 compares a candle with itself, which is always zero percent.
refusal.operandDimensionMismatch: The two sides of this condition are denominated differently — traded volume against something that is not volume. Compare volume against a volume average or against a plain threshold.
refusal.nestedWindow: A window over a window is not supported. Aggregate over a plain value instead — a lowest high or a highest low, not a lowest highest.
refusal.invalidWindowLookback: A window needs at least 2 closes and at most 500. One close is the value itself, and deeper history cannot be loaded reliably.
refusal.cumulativeNeedsOwnWindow: OBV is a running total, so its level depends on how much history is loaded. Compare it only with its own highest or lowest value over a number of candles.
refusal.ruleWarmupTooDeep: This rule needs more closed candles than the app can load. Shorten the window or use a shorter indicator period — otherwise the alert would stay silent instead of firing.
refusal.invalidNote: The note in `{field}` is empty or longer than 280 characters.
refusal.invalidDerivedFromHash: The derivation in `{field}` is not a valid content hash, so the strategy this was promoted from cannot be identified.
refusal.duplicateTriggerMethod: A trigger channel is listed twice in `{field}`, which would announce the same trigger twice.
refusal.stopRequiredForRiskSizing: `{field}` is missing: a size given as percent of risk is measured between the entry and the stop, so it has no value until the stop is set.
refusal.stopNotHonoured: `{field}` would never be placed: a reduce-only order closes an existing position rather than opening one that needs protecting.
